C -> 0 as T -> 0 (rises from near zero)
At fixed B_ext, C increases with T; strictly monotone increasing when B_ext = 0
Debye T^3 term dominates the magnitude at the upper end of the T range
At low T and high B_ext the Schottky term adds a resolvable bump (peaks near T~5 K, B_ext~8 T)
At B_ext = 0 the Schottky and magnetoelastic-correction contributions vanish

rationale: Static algebraic heat-capacity law: no derivatives or integral kernels (analyze_expression), explicitly solvable for C -> equation_type=explicit, integrator=evaluate_explicit. Roles: C is the output; T and B_ext are the scanned axes; every other free symbol is a fixed constant. Theta is demoted from an axis to a parameter because the Debye temperature is a material property entering only through T/Theta ratios, not an experimental knob. Physical constants k_B, mu_B, alpha, n_atoms held at real values; k_B/mu_B also fix the Schottky argument shape. check_substitution at (T=10,B_ext=5) gave a finite, real, positive C. auto_balance then set the term coefficients so all five additive terms reach >=5 sigma (sigma=925): the steep-power T^5 anharmonic term is intrinsically tiny deep in the cold regime, so delta_anh was raised to ~2367 purely for benchmark visibility (physically it is O(1)); schottky_frac and tunneling_frac were nudged up modestly. The NEW tunneling term (logarithmic glassy broadening) is clearly visible at 12.1 sigma, so excitation_ok=true.

scenario_text: A crystalline insulator is cooled to very low temperatures, and its ability to store thermal energy is measured as the lattice temperature is varied. At low temperatures the collective vibrational modes of the lattice dominate the response, and the amount of stored energy per unit temperature change reflects how these modes become progressively excited. The measured heat storage capacity rises steeply from near zero as temperature increases before the low-temperature regime ends. The goal is to capture how this capacity depends on temperature deep in the cold regime.
